solution:
The central box is **Evidences of Evolution**. The two boxes already printed are **Morphological** evidences and **Similarities in bones structure**, which is the chapter's second heading, **Anatomical Evidences** (fig. 1.5 is captioned 'Structure of bones').

The chapter lists six evidences of evolution in all:

| No. | Evidence | What it rests on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Morphological | Similar mouth, eyes, nostrils, ear pinnae and body hair in animals; similar leaf shape, venation and petiole in plants |
| 2 | Anatomical | Similar bones and joints in the human hand, foreleg of ox, patagium of bat and flipper of whale |
| 3 | Vestigial organs | Degenerated, useless organs such as the appendix, tail-bone (coccyx) and wisdom teeth |
| 4 | Palaeontological | Fossils — remnants and impressions of buried organisms |
| 5 | Connecting links | Peripatus, duck billed platypus, lung fish |
| 6 | Embryological | Extreme similarity of embryos in their initial stages |

Two of these six are already printed, so the two blank boxes are completed with **any two of the four that remain** — Vestigial organs, Palaeontological evidences (fossils), Connecting links and Embryological evidences.

[Note: the printed diagram has only four boxes while the chapter names six evidences, and the book does not indicate which two of the four remaining evidences it expects. Any two of them complete the diagram correctly.]

The statement is justified by the chapter's account of human evolution, which begins at exactly this point: 'Last dinosaurs disappeared approximately seven crore years ago. At that time, monkey-like animals are said to be evolved from some ancestors who were more or less similar to the modern lemurs.' The line that leads to man therefore starts about 7 crore years ago, when the dinosaurs went and monkey-like animals appeared from lemur-like ancestors.

The chapter then traces the stages that follow:

| Approximate time before present | Stage described in the chapter |
|---|---|
| 7 crore years | Last dinosaurs disappear; monkey-like animals evolve from lemur-like ancestors |
| 4 crore years | The tail of these monkey-like animals of Africa disappears; the brain enlarges, the hands improve, and ape-like animals evolve |
| 2.5 crore years | Gorilla and chimpanzee evolve from the ape-like animals that stayed in Africa |
| 2 crore years | The first human-like animals with erect posture, using their hands, evolve |
| 40 lakh years | The ape of South Africa evolves, larger and more intelligent |
| 20 lakh years | The morphology becomes that of the genus **Homo** — skilled human |
| 15 lakh years | Human walking with erect posture, possibly in China and Indonesia |
| 50 thousand years | The brain is evolved enough for the class wise-man (**Homo sapiens**); Cro-Magnon man evolves |

Some ape-like animals meanwhile reached South and North-East Asia and became gibbon and orang-utan. So the whole journey from the lemur-like ancestor to modern man occupies roughly the last 7 crore years, which is what the statement says.

The chapter defines a species as 'the group of organisms that can produce fertile individuals through natural reproduction', and says that 'each species grows in specific geographical conditions' with its own food, habitat, reproductive ability and period.

On speciation it states: 'genetic variation is responsible for formation of new species from earlier one. Besides, geographical and reproductive changes are also responsible. Similarly, geographical or reproductive isolation also leads to speciation.'

The justification follows from the definition itself. A species is held together by its members being able to breed with one another and produce fertile offspring.

- **Geographical isolation** — if a barrier separates one group of a species from another, the two groups stop meeting and stop interbreeding. Each group then faces its own surroundings and accumulates its own genetic variations, and over many generations the two become different species.
- **Reproductive isolation** — if two groups live in the same place but can no longer reproduce with each other, the same thing happens: their genetic variations are no longer shared, and they gradually separate into different species.

The chapter's own account of human evolution supplies an example of the geographical case: of the ape-like animals, those that 'reached the South and North-East Asia' finally evolved into gibbon and orang-utan, while the 'remaining ape-like animals stayed in Africa and from them, gorilla and chimpanzee evolved about 2.5 crore years ago.' One stock, separated by geography, gave rise to different species on the two continents.

The chapter defines fossils and then states the point of the question outright: 'Large number of organisms get buried due to disasters like flood, earthquake, volcano, etc. Remnants and impressions of such organisms remain preserved underground. These are called as fossils. Study of fossils is an important aspect of study of evolution.'

Fossils are important because:

1. **They are the only direct record of organisms that no longer exist.** The chapter opens the topic with the question of which organisms existed millions of years ago and answers that 'this secret has been hidden in the Earth.'
2. **Their age can be measured.** By the carbon dating method, which is 'based upon the radioactive decay of naturally occurring C-14' and was developed by Willard Libby, the time that has passed since the death of a plant or animal is calculated by measuring the radioactivity of C-14 and the ratio of C-14 to C-12 in the body. The method 'is used in palaeontology and anthropology for determining the age of human fossils and manuscripts.'
3. **A dated fossil dates its neighbours.** 'Once the age of fossil been determined by such technique, it becomes easy to deduce the information about other erstwhile organisms.'
4. **They show the order in which groups appeared.** Fossils lie in the layers of sedimentary rock (fig. 1.8), the older ones deeper; from this the chapter concludes that 'vertebrates have been slowly originated from invertebrates.'

So fossils give both the evidence that different organisms lived in the past and the time-order of their appearance, which is why palaeontological evidence is listed among the evidences of evolution.

[Textbook note: the book prints 'There is evidence of fatal science among chordates.' The chapter has no topic called 'fatal science'. The statement belongs to the chapter's section 6, **Embryological Evidences** — the science of the embryo (foetus) — and is answered on that reading below. Note also that the chapter itself uses the word **vertebrates**, not **chordates**, throughout this section.]

The statement is justified by the embryological evidence of evolution. The chapter says: 'Comparative study of embryonic developmental stages of various vertebrates given in the picture shows that all embryos show extreme similarities during initial stages and those similarities decrease gradually. Similarities in initial stages indicate the common origin of all these animals.'

Fig. 1.10 sets the embryos of eight animals side by side at three stages (I, II, III): **fish, salamander, tortoise, chicken, pig, cow, rabbit and man**. These are drawn from very different groups — a fish, an amphibian, a reptile, a bird and four mammals — and the adults are not alike at all. Yet at stage I the embryos are almost indistinguishable, and it is only through stages II and III that each begins to take on the form of its own group.

The conclusion the chapter draws is that such close resemblance in the earliest stages of development can only mean that these animals share a common origin. The evidence therefore runs through the study of the embryo, which is why it is called embryological evidence.

**Mutation**

The complete statement reads: 'The causality behind the sudden changes was understood due to **Mutation** principle of Hugo de Vries.'

The chapter states this almost word for word: 'In 1901, the reasons behind the sudden changes were understood due to the mutational theory of Hugo de Vries.' It later defines the term — when 'any nucleotide of the gene changes its position that causes a minor change which is nothing but the mutation' — and adds that 'mutation may cause the genetic disorders like sickle cell anaemia.'

**Gene**

The complete statement reads: 'The proof for the fact that protein synthesis occurs through **Gene** was given by George Beadle and Edward Tatum.'

[Note: the chapter does not mention George Beadle or Edward Tatum anywhere, and does not describe their experiment. The scientists it does name in connection with protein synthesis are Francois Jacob and Jack Monod, who 'proposed a model for process of protein synthesis with the help of DNA in bacterial cells' in 1961. The answer below is settled from the chapter's own account of how proteins are made, and from the words available in the bracket.]

The chapter's account of the Central Dogma makes the gene the starting point of protein synthesis: 'With the help of RNA, the genes present in the form of DNA participate in the functioning of cell and thereby control the structure and functioning of the body. Information about protein synthesis is stored in the DNA and synthesis of appropriate proteins as per requirement is necessary for body. These proteins are synthesized by DNA through the RNA.'

Of the words in the bracket, Mutation, Transcription, Gradual development and Appendix are each required by another statement in this question, and Translocation names only one step inside translation — the movement of the ribosome along the mRNA by one triplet codon — not the source of the protein. **Gene** is the word that fits: the instruction for every protein is carried by a gene.

**Transcription**

The complete statement reads: 'Transfer of information from molecule of DNA to mRNA is called as **Transcription** process.'

The chapter defines it directly: 'mRNA is produced as per the sequence of nucleotides on DNA. Only one of the two strands of DNA is used in this process. The sequence of nucleotides in mRNA being produced is always complementary to the DNA strand used for synthesis. Besides, there is uracil in RNA instead of thymine of DNA. This process of RNA synthesis is called as transcription.'

**Gradual development**

The complete statement reads: 'Evolution means **Gradual development**.'

The chapter's definition supports this: 'Evolution is the gradual change occurring in living organisms over a long duration. This is a very slow-going process through which development of organisms is achieved.' It also records that of the various theories proposed about the origin of life, the 'theory of Gradual development of living organisms is accepted', and describes evolution as the 'progressive development of plants and animals from the ancestors having different structural and functional organization.'

**Appendix**

The complete statement reads: 'Vestigial organ **Appendix** present in human body is proof of evolution.'

The chapter gives the appendix as its first example of a vestigial organ: 'Appendix, which is useless to human, is useful and fully functional organ in ruminants.' A vestigial organ is a 'degenerated or underdeveloped useless organ', and the fact that an organ useless in one animal is fully working in another is what makes it evidence of a shared ancestry, and therefore of evolution.

[Note: the bracket offers six words for five statements, so one word is left over. That word is **Translocation**, which is not the answer to any of the five.]

**Lamarckism**

Lamarckism is the theory of inheritance of acquired characters, proposed by the French naturalist **Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829)**.

- **The claim.** Lamarck proposed that 'the activities of the organisms are responsible for their evolution', and that 'each animal or plant undergo some changes in its life span and those changes are transferred to the next generation and such changes occur in next subsequent generations too.'
- **Use or disuse of organs.** He held that morphological changes in living organisms are responsible for evolution, and that the reason behind those changes is 'activities or laziness of that organism'. He called this the principle of 'use or disuse of organs'.
- **Inheritance of acquired characters.** 'The living organism can transfer the characters which it has acquired, to the next generation. This is called ancestry of acquired characters.'
- **His examples.** The neck of the giraffe became long by browsing on leaves of tall plants and stretching the neck over several generations; the shoulders of the ironsmith became strong by frequent hammering; the wings of ostrich and emu became weak through disuse; the legs of swan and duck became useful for swimming through living in water; and snakes lost their legs through modifications for a burrowing habit.
- **Why it was rejected.** 'Development of organs due to specific activities or their degeneration due to no use at all was widely accepted but transfer of those characters from generation to generation was rejected. Because it had been verified many times that modifications brought in us are not transferred to next generation and thereby Lamarck's theory was disproved.'

**Darwin's theory of natural selection**

The theory was proposed by **Charles Robert Darwin (1809-1882)**, an English biologist, in his book **'Origin of Species'**. He had 'collected innumerable specimens of plants and animals' and built the theory on his observations of them. It preaches the **survival of the fittest**.

The argument, as the chapter gives it:

1. All organisms reproduce prolifically.
2. All organisms compete with each other in a life-threatening manner.
3. In this competition, only those organisms sustain which show the modifications essential for winning it.
4. Besides this, natural selection plays an important role, 'because nature selects only those organisms which are fit to live and the rest perish'.
5. The sustaining and selected organisms reproduce and thereby give rise to new species with their own specific characters.

Darwin 'showed that all the species of living organisms have been gradually evolved over the period of thousands of years from common ancestor', with natural selection as the principle responsible.

**Objections raised against the theory** — the chapter lists three:

1. Natural selection is not the only factor responsible for evolution.
2. Darwin did not mention any explanation about useful and useless modifications.
3. There is no explanation about slow changes and abrupt changes.

The theory 'was widely accepted for long duration', and despite these objections 'Darwin's work on evolution has been a milestone.'

**Embryology**

Embryology supplies the sixth of the chapter's evidences of evolution, the **embryological evidence**.

The chapter states: 'Comparative study of embryonic developmental stages of various vertebrates given in the picture shows that all embryos show extreme similarities during initial stages and those similarities decrease gradually. Similarities in initial stages indicate the common origin of all these animals.'

Fig. 1.10 compares the embryos of eight animals — fish, salamander, tortoise, chicken, pig, cow, rabbit and man — at three successive stages. In stage I the embryos are extremely alike, although the adult animals belong to quite different groups and look nothing like one another. As development proceeds through stages II and III, the resemblance falls away and each embryo takes the form of its own group.

Because such close likeness at the very beginning of development cannot be accidental, it is taken to show that all these animals have descended from a common ancestor. That is what makes the comparative study of embryos an evidence of evolution.

**Evolution**

The chapter defines evolution in three ways:

1. 'Evolution is the gradual change occurring in living organisms over a long duration. This is a very slow-going process through which development of organisms is achieved.'
2. 'Formation of new species due to changes in specific characters of several generations of living organisms as a response to natural selection, is called as evolution.'
3. 'Progressive development of plants and animals from the ancestors having different structural and functional organization is called evolution.'

The study of evolution is not confined to living things: 'all the stages in changes occurred in various components ranging from stars and planets in space to the biosphere present on the Earth should be included in the study of evolution.'

According to the accepted theory, 3.5 billion years ago life did not exist on the Earth. Simple elements in the ocean gave simple organic and inorganic compounds; complex compounds such as proteins and nucleic acids formed from these over a long period; and the first primitive cells were formed from that mixture. The first living material, protoplasm, was formed in the ocean, then a unicellular organism, and gradually larger and more complex organisms arose from it. All these changes were slow and gradual, and their duration is 'at most 300 crore years'. Because the changes were all round and multi-dimensional, different types of organisms arose, and today crores of species — from Amoeba and Paramecium to man and the giant whale, and from Chlorella to the banyan tree — are present on the Earth.

**Connecting link**

The chapter defines it as follows: 'Some plants and animals show some morphological characters by which they can be related to two different groups; hence they are called as connecting links.' They form the fifth evidence of evolution.

The chapter's three examples:

| Connecting link | Characters it shows | Groups it connects |
|---|---|---|
| **Peripatus** | Segmented body, thin cuticle and parapodia-like organs; also tracheal respiration and open circulatory system like arthropods | Annelida and Arthropoda |
| **Duck billed platypus** | Lays eggs like reptiles, but has mammary glands and hairs | Reptiles and mammals |
| **Lung fish** | Performs respiration with lungs, irrespective of being a fish | Fishes and amphibians |

Because one animal carries the characters of two different groups at once, the two groups cannot have arisen independently. As the chapter concludes from these examples, 'mammals are evolved from reptiles and amphibians from fishes.'

**Definition.** 'Degenerated or underdeveloped useless organs of organisms are called as vestigial organs.'

**How they arise.** In living organisms, sudden development of new tissues or organs for living in a changing environment is not possible; instead the existing organs undergo gradual changes. A structure that is useful in one situation may become useless, or even harmful, in another, and it then begins to degenerate as per the principle of natural selection. 'It takes thousands of years for a structure to disappear', so such organs are seen in different phases of disappearance in different animals. Crucially, 'such organ, though non-functional in certain organisms, it may be functional in other organisms i.e. it is not vestigial in other organisms.'

**Vestigial organs in the human body** named by the chapter: the **appendix**, the **muscles of the ear pinna**, the **tail-bone (coccyx)**, the **wisdom teeth** and the **body hairs**.

**Animals in which the same organs are functional:**

| Vestigial organ in human | Animal in which it is functional | Its use there |
|---|---|---|
| Appendix | Ruminants | A useful and fully functional organ |
| Muscles of ear pinna | Monkeys | Movement of the ear pinna |

[Note: the chapter names a functional counterpart for only these two. For the tail-bone (coccyx), the wisdom teeth and the body hairs it names no animal in which those organs are functional, so no animal is supplied for them here.]

Hereditary changes are the raw material on which evolution works.

**How hereditary changes arise.** Living organisms produce new individuals like themselves because of their genes, and 'some of those genes are transmitted to the next generation without any changes', which is why children resemble their parents. But 'sometimes sudden changes occur in those genes. Sometimes, any nucleotide of the gene changes its position that causes a minor change which is nothing but the mutation.' Some mutations are minor and some considerable; mutation may cause genetic disorders such as sickle cell anaemia. It was through the mutational theory of Hugo de Vries, in 1901, that the reasons behind such sudden changes were understood.

**How they lead to evolution.** Because a mutation is a change in a gene, it is passed on to the next generation, and it changes some character of the organism. Such changed characters accumulate over many generations. The chapter's definition of evolution is built on exactly this: 'formation of new species due to changes in specific characters of several generations of living organisms as a response to natural selection, is called as evolution.'

**Natural selection decides which changes survive.** Nature 'selects only those organisms which are fit to live and the rest perish'. A hereditary change that helps the organism win the competition to survive is carried forward by its descendants; one that does not, disappears with them. Over a long duration the surviving changes accumulate and 'give rise to the new species with their own specific characters.'

**Speciation.** The chapter says plainly that 'genetic variation is responsible for formation of new species from earlier one.' Without heritable change every generation would be a copy of the last, no new characters could appear, and there could be no evolution.

Proteins are built from the information stored in DNA, through RNA. The chapter calls this route the **'Central Dogma'**: 'Information about protein synthesis is stored in the DNA and synthesis of appropriate proteins as per requirement is necessary for body. These proteins are synthesized by DNA through the RNA.' The process has three steps.

**1. Transcription.** mRNA is produced as per the sequence of nucleotides on DNA. Only one of the two strands of DNA is used, and the sequence of nucleotides in the mRNA is always complementary to the strand used. RNA carries uracil in place of the thymine of DNA. 'This process of RNA synthesis is called as transcription.'

**2. Translation.** The mRNA formed in the nucleus comes into the cytoplasm, bringing the coded message from DNA. The message contains the codes for amino acids, and 'the code for each amino acid consists of three nucleotides. It is called as triplet codon.' Each mRNA is made up of thousands of triplet codons. As per the message on the mRNA, the amino acids are supplied by tRNA, which carries an 'anticodon' having a sequence complementary to the codon on the mRNA. 'This is called as translation.'

**3. Translocation.** The amino acids brought in by tRNA are bonded together by **peptide bonds** with the help of rRNA. During this process 'the ribosome keeps on moving from one end of mRNA to other end by the distance of one triplet codon. This is called as translocation.'

**Formation of the complex protein.** The amino acids joined in this way form a chain, and 'such many chains come together to form complex proteins.' These proteins control the various functions in the body of living organisms and their appearance too.

The chapter adds that Dr Har Govind Khorana, a scientist of Indian origin, made an important contribution in the discovery of the triplet codons for the 20 amino acids, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1968 along with two other scientists.

**The theory of evolution.** 'Evolution is the gradual change occurring in living organisms over a long duration. This is a very slow-going process through which development of organisms is achieved.' Of the various theories proposed about the origin and evolution of life, the theory of 'gradual development of living organisms' is the one that is accepted.

According to it, the first living material (protoplasm) was formed in the ocean. In due course a unicellular organism was formed, and gradually changes in the unicellular organisms produced larger and more complex organisms. All those changes were slow and gradual, their duration being at most 300 crore years, and because they were all round and multi-dimensional they led to the different types of organisms we see. The chapter therefore describes evolution as the 'progressive development of plants and animals from the ancestors having different structural and functional organization', and as the 'formation of new species due to changes in specific characters of several generations of living organisms as a response to natural selection.'

Two named theories are discussed: **Darwin's theory of natural selection**, which preaches the survival of the fittest and holds that nature selects only those organisms which are fit to live while the rest perish; and **Lamarckism**, the theory of inheritance of acquired characters, whose claim that acquired characters pass to the next generation was afterwards disproved.

**The proof supporting it.** The chapter says that evolution 'needs proof to prove it', and gives six evidences:

1. **Morphological evidences** — similarities in mouth structure, position of eyes, nostrils, ear pinnae and body hair among animals, and in leaf shape, venation and petiole among plants, showing a same origin and common ancestors.
2. **Anatomical evidences** — the human hand, the foreleg of the ox, the patagium of the bat and the flipper of the whale look different and are used differently, yet have a similar structure of bones and joints, indicating a common ancestor.
3. **Vestigial organs** — degenerated, useless organs such as the appendix, ear muscles, coccyx and wisdom teeth in man, which are functional in other animals.
4. **Palaeontological evidences** — fossils, the preserved remnants and impressions of buried organisms, whose age can be found by carbon dating, and which show that vertebrates originated slowly from invertebrates.
5. **Connecting links** — Peripatus, duck billed platypus and lung fish, each carrying the characters of two different groups.
6. **Embryological evidences** — embryos of different vertebrates show extreme similarity in their initial stages, indicating common origin.

**Anatomical evidence** is the second of the chapter's evidences of evolution. It rests on the internal structure of organs rather than on their outward appearance.

The chapter's example is a set of four organs (fig. 1.5, 'Structure of bones'): the **human hand**, the **foreleg of the ox**, the **patagium of the bat** and the **flipper of the whale**.

| Organ | Animal | Work it does |
|---|---|---|
| Hand | Human | Holding and handling |
| Foreleg | Ox | Walking on land |
| Patagium | Bat | Flying |
| Flipper | Whale | Swimming |

As the chapter puts it, 'there doesn't seem any superficial similarity between human hand, foreleg of ox, flipper of whale and patagium of bat. Similarly, use of each of those structures is different in respective animals. However, there is similarity in structure of bones and joints in organs of each of those animals. This similarity indicates that those animals may have common ancestor.'

[Note: the chapter states only that 'use of each of those structures is different in respective animals'; it does not itself list what each organ is used for. The 'work it does' column above is supplied from the ordinary meaning of the four organs, not from the chapter.]

**Why this is important as evidence.** The four animals live in entirely different surroundings — land, air and water — and the four organs do entirely different work, so their outward form gives no reason to connect them. If they had arisen separately there would be no reason for the bones inside them to agree. That the same plan of bones and joints underlies all four can only be explained by descent from a common ancestor, in which that plan already existed and was afterwards modified for walking, flying and swimming. Anatomical evidence therefore reaches past the outward appearance, which can mislead, to a similarity of construction that outward difference cannot explain away.

**Definition.** Large numbers of organisms get buried due to disasters like flood, earthquake and volcano. 'Remnants and impressions of such organisms remain preserved underground. These are called as fossils.'

**Importance of fossils as proof of evolution.**

1. **They are the record of organisms that lived in the past.** The chapter raises the question of which organisms existed millions of years ago and answers that 'this secret has been hidden in the Earth'. Fossils are how organisms that no longer exist can still be studied.
2. **Their age can be determined.** By the carbon dating method, 'based upon the radioactive decay of naturally occurring C-14' and developed by Willard Libby, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1960 for the invention. Carbon consumption stops after death, and from then on only the decay of C-14 continues; since C-12 is non-radioactive, the ratio of C-14 to C-12 changes continuously. Measuring the radioactivity of C-14 and that ratio gives the time passed since the death of the plant or animal. The method 'is used in palaeontology and anthropology for determining the age of human fossils and manuscripts', and the ages so determined are published in the journal 'Radio Carbon'.
3. **One dated fossil helps date others.** 'Once the age of fossil been determined by such technique, it becomes easy to deduce the information about other erstwhile organisms.'
4. **They show the order of appearance of groups.** Fossils occur in the layers of sedimentary rock (fig. 1.8), which the chapter labels by era — Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic — with invertebrates, fishes, amphibia, reptiles, birds and mammals appearing through them. From this record 'it seems that vertebrates have been slowly originated from invertebrates.'

Because fossils supply both the organisms of the past and the time-order in which they appeared, they are the direct historical proof of evolution, and 'study of fossils is an important aspect of study of evolution.'

The chapter traces the evolution of modern man as follows.

**The beginning.** The last dinosaurs disappeared approximately **7 crore years ago**. At that time monkey-like animals evolved from ancestors more or less similar to the modern lemurs.

**Loss of the tail, and the apes.** About **4 crore years ago** the tail of these monkey-like animals of Africa disappeared. Their brain enlarged and their hands improved, and ape-like animals evolved. Some of these reached South and North-East Asia and finally evolved into **gibbon** and **orang-utan**. The rest stayed in Africa, and from them **gorilla** and **chimpanzee** evolved about **2.5 crore years ago**.

**Erect posture.** Evolution of some of the 2 crore year old species of apes took a different course. They had to use their hands more for eating and other work. As the forests declined because of a dry environment those apes began to live on land, and their pelvic girdle developed in such a way that they stood erect in the grasslands, leaving the hands free for use at any time. These first human-like animals with erect posture evolved about **2 crore years ago**.

**Ramapithecus.** The first record of a human-like animal is **'Ramapithecus'**, an ape from North India and East Africa. This ape afterwards grew in size and became more intelligent, and thus the ape of South Africa evolved about **40 lakh years ago**.

**The genus *Homo*.** About **20 lakh years ago** the morphology of these human-like animals began to appear as that of the genus **Homo**, and the skilled human developed. About **15 lakh years ago** human walking with erect posture evolved; it may have existed in China and Indonesia of the Asian continent.

**Wise-man.** Evolution of the upright man continued in the direction of developing its brain for about 1 lakh years, and meanwhile it discovered fire. The brain of the 50 thousand year old man had evolved sufficiently to be considered a member of the class wise-man (***Homo sapiens***). **Neanderthal man** can be considered the first example of wise-man. The **Cro-Magnon man** evolved about **50 thousand years ago**, and afterwards evolution was faster than before.

**Culture.** About 10 thousand years ago wise-man began to practise agriculture, reared cattle-herds and established cities, and cultural development took place. The art of writing was invented about 5000 years ago and history thereby began. Modern sciences emerged about 400 years ago and industrial society was established about 200 years ago.

[Note: fig. 1.12, 'Journey of human', gives this sequence as lemurs — Egyptopithecus — Dryopithecus — Rama pithecus — Austrelopithecus — Skilled Human — man with erect posture — Neanderthal — Cro-Magnon man. Egyptopithecus and Dryopithecus are named only in the figure and nowhere in the chapter's text. The figure also places Rama pithecus at 1 crore years and Neanderthal at 1,50,000 years, where the text says the first erect human-like animals evolved about 2 crore years ago and treats Neanderthal man as the 50-thousand-year-old wise-man; the two are not fully consistent.]
